solution.concept_anchor: Policy Cut vs Token Cut vs Economy Cut distinction
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students often associate 'reduction to Re. 1' with a symbolic grievance, not understanding it signals wholesale policy rejection.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Reduction to Re. 1 is the Policy Cut Motion signalling policy disapproval, not a grievance ventilation mechanism.
Eliminate (c): A reduction by Rs. 100 is the Token Cut — it raises a specific grievance, not a comment on economy of expenditure.
Eliminate (d): Economy Cut specifies a rupee amount for economy — it does not reduce to Re. 1.
Retain (b): The Economy Cut Motion proposes reduction by a specific stated amount to signal that proposed expenditure is excessive — this is correct.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Students frequently conflate the three types of cut motions because all three involve 'reducing' a demand. The trap here is that 'reduction to Re. 1' sounds like the most drastic cut and is therefore mistaken for either expressing the greatest grievance or seeking maximum economy. In reality, Re. 1 reduction is the Policy Cut that signals disapproval of the policy behind the demand. The Token Cut (Rs. 100) is purely for airing a specific grievance, while the Economy Cut specifies an actual rupee figure to flag wasteful expenditure.
solution.final_explanation:
Cut motions are parliamentary instruments to oppose specific demands for grants. Understanding which type does what is a perennial UPSC trap.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Reduction to Re. 1 is the Policy Cut Motion. It symbolically conveys that Parliament disapproves of the policy underlying the demand — not that a specific grievance is being raised.
• Option (b) — Correct: The Economy Cut Motion proposes reducing a demand by a specific stated amount, implying that the proposed expenditure is excessive or wasteful. The amount must be explicitly mentioned in the motion.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: A reduction by Rs. 100 is the Token Cut Motion. Its purpose is to ventilate a specific public grievance within the government's domain — it is purely symbolic.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The Policy Cut reduces to Re. 1, not by a specific rupee figure.

Value Addition:
• Policy Cut → Re. 1 → policy disapproval; Token Cut → Rs. 100 → specific grievance; Economy Cut → specific amount → wasteful expenditure.
• All three apply only at the Voting on Demands for Grants stage in Lok Sabha.
• Passage of any cut motion is technically a defeat for the government on that demand.

solution.concept_anchor: Admissibility conditions for cut motions

statement_analysis.statement: A cut motion is admissible if it relates to expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India.
statement_analysis.reason: Charged expenditure — such as the salaries of the President, CAG, and Supreme Court judges — is non-votable and therefore cannot be the subject of a cut motion.

statement_analysis.statement: A cut motion must relate to one demand only and must not contain arguments or inferences.
statement_analysis.reason: The Rules of Procedure of Lok Sabha require that a cut motion pertain to a single demand and be clearly expressed without arguments, inferences, or defamatory language.

statement_analysis.statement: A cut motion is inadmissible if it refers to a matter that is pending before any statutory tribunal.
statement_analysis.reason: One of the explicit admissibility conditions is that the cut motion must not relate to matters sub judice before courts or statutory tribunals.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1 and 3 only' is a strong distractor because students who correctly identify Statement 1 as wrong may still incorrectly recall that sub-judice matters are permissible, causing them to exclude Statement 3.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Charged expenditure (President's salary, CAG salary, judges' salaries) is non-votable — cut motions cannot apply to it. Statement 1 is INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: The single-demand rule and prohibition on arguments are standard admissibility conditions in Lok Sabha Rules 209–221. Statement 2 is CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3: Sub-judice matters before courts or statutory tribunals are explicitly excluded from cut motions. Statement 3 is CORRECT.
Only Statements 2 and 3 are correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 exploits the common misconception that all items in the Union Budget are subject to cut motions. Students who have not carefully distinguished 'charged' from 'voted' expenditure will mark Statement 1 as correct, leading them away from option (b). The Constitution (Article 113) makes this distinction explicit — charged expenditure is placed outside the vote of Parliament precisely to protect constitutional functionaries' independence.
solution.final_explanation:
Admissibility of cut motions is governed by Rules 209–221 of the Lok Sabha Rules of Procedure, and several conditions restrict what can be targeted.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Charged expenditure items are placed outside the purview of a vote by Parliament under Article 113. The salaries of the President, CAG, Supreme Court and High Court judges, and debt servicing charges fall into this category. Cut motions can only target 'voted' demands for grants.
• Statement 2 — Correct: A cut motion must be confined to a single demand, clearly expressed, and free of arguments, inferences, ironical expressions, or defamatory content.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Matters sub judice before a court of law or statutory tribunal are explicitly inadmissible as subjects of a cut motion — Parliament should not pre-empt ongoing judicial proceedings.

Value Addition:
• Charged items include: salary of President, VP, Speaker, Deputy Speaker, CAG, Supreme Court & High Court judges, and debt charges of India.
• A cut motion that violates any admissibility condition can be disallowed by the Speaker.
• The Speaker has discretionary power to modify the scope of a cut motion before admitting it.

solution.concept_anchor: Cut motions restricted to Lok Sabha only

statement_analysis.statement: Rajya Sabha members may move cut motions on demands for grants as part of their role in scrutinising the Union Budget.
statement_analysis.reason: Under Article 109, Rajya Sabha has no power to vote on demands for grants. Cut motions can only be moved in Lok Sabha.

statement_analysis.statement: The constitutional basis for excluding Rajya Sabha from voting on demands for grants is found in Article 109 of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 109 specifically deals with Money Bills and establishes that Rajya Sabha cannot amend or reject Money Bills — it can only make recommendations, which Lok Sabha may choose to accept or reject.

statement_analysis.statement: Rajya Sabha's recommendations on a Money Bill are binding on the Lok Sabha if not acted upon within fourteen days.
statement_analysis.reason: Rajya Sabha's recommendations on a Money Bill are not binding. If Lok Sabha does not act on them, the Bill is deemed passed by both Houses in the form Lok Sabha passed it.

solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) '2 only' is a strong distractor because Statement 2 is genuinely correct, and students may focus only on it while overlooking that Statement 3 is also incorrect, making (b) insufficient.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Rajya Sabha has no power over demands for grants (Article 109) — cut motions are exclusively a Lok Sabha instrument. Statement 1 is INCORRECT — qualifies as 'not correct'.
Evaluate Statement 2: Article 109 is indeed the constitutional provision restricting Rajya Sabha's role on Money Bills. Statement 2 is CORRECT — does not qualify.
Evaluate Statement 3: Rajya Sabha's recommendations on a Money Bill are never binding; the Bill is deemed passed in Lok Sabha's form after 14 days. Statement 3 is INCORRECT — qualifies.
Statements 1 and 3 are NOT correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a classic scope-extension trap. Students know Rajya Sabha has a 14-day window for Money Bills but often misremember whether its recommendations become binding after that period. The answer is no — non-action by Lok Sabha simply means the Bill is deemed passed as originally sent, reinforcing Lok Sabha's financial supremacy.
solution.final_explanation:
The financial supremacy of Lok Sabha over Rajya Sabha is a foundational constitutional design. Article 109 places Money Bills — including demands for grants — firmly within Lok Sabha's exclusive domain.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Rajya Sabha has zero power to vote on demands for grants. Cut motions are a Lok Sabha prerogative. A Rajya Sabha member cannot move a cut motion.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 109 is the correct constitutional basis. It provides that Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations on Money Bills within 14 days; Lok Sabha may accept or reject them.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Rajya Sabha's recommendations are advisory, not binding. If Lok Sabha does not adopt them, the Bill passes in the form Lok Sabha originally passed it — the 14-day clock does not convert recommendations into amendments.

Value Addition:
• Similarly, in state legislatures, only the Vidhan Sabha (not Vidhan Parishad) can move cut motions on state budget demands.
• Article 110 defines what constitutes a Money Bill; the Speaker's certification is final.
• Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved; hence it has no direct role in budget passage.

solution.concept_anchor: Three types of cut motions matched to purpose and amount
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it correctly places the Policy Cut at A-2 but swaps Token Cut and Economy Cut, which many students confuse due to both involving symbolic or small amounts.
elimination_logic: Anchor match: Policy Cut Motion (A) reduces demand to Re. 1 to signal policy disapproval — matches item 2 (reduction to Re. 1, policy disapproval). A-2 is confirmed.
Economy Cut Motion (B) proposes reduction by a specific stated amount citing wasteful expenditure — matches item 3. B-3 is confirmed.
Token Cut Motion (C) reduces demand by Rs. 100 to ventilate a specific grievance — matches item 1. C-1 is confirmed.
The guillotine (D) refers to the mechanism whereby undiscussed demands are put to vote at the close of allotted time — matches item 4. D-4 is confirmed. Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The classic trap is swapping the Token Cut (Rs. 100, specific grievance) with the Economy Cut (specific amount, excessive expenditure). Both involve 'a reduction' and students who have not memorised the exact definitions will conflate them. The Policy Cut's 'Re. 1' is usually recalled correctly, making A-2 the anchor — but the swap of B and C misleads those who rely on partial memory.
solution.final_explanation:
The three types of cut motions are distinguished by the amount of reduction proposed and the purpose behind it. The guillotine is a related procedural device.

• A (Policy Cut) — 2: Reducing a demand to Re. 1 signals that Parliament disapproves of the policy underlying that demand. The symbolic Re. 1 represents total policy rejection.
• B (Economy Cut) — 3: A specific rupee amount is proposed as a reduction to indicate that the projected expenditure is wasteful or excessive. The amount must be stated in the motion itself.
• C (Token Cut) — 1: A reduction of Rs. 100 is purely symbolic and is used to raise a specific grievance within the government's sphere of responsibility.
• D (Guillotine) — 4: When the allotted time for discussing demands for grants expires, all undiscussed demands — along with any pending cut motions — are put to vote together without debate.

Value Addition:
• The guillotine renders most cut motions ineffective in practice since they never reach discussion.
• Guillotine as a parliamentary device originated in the UK Parliament.
• Departmentally Related Standing Committees are considered a more effective tool for financial scrutiny than cut motions.

solution.concept_anchor: Charged expenditure immunity from cut motions — Article 113
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because both A and R are factually correct, and students may hastily assume that the reason (Article 113) causally explains the assertion without checking whether Article 113 is actually about charged vs. voted distinction.
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes. Expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India — such as the salary of the CAG — cannot be subjected to a cut motion because it is non-votable.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? No. Article 113 distinguishes between charged and voted expenditure and specifies that charged items shall not be submitted to the vote of Parliament. This is accurate — R is correct as a fact.
Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? Yes. The reason that charged expenditure is immune from cut motions is precisely Article 113, which places it outside Parliament's voting power. R does explain A.
Both A and R are correct and R explains A — select option (a).
solution.final_explanation:
The distinction between charged and voted expenditure is constitutionally significant and directly governs the applicability of cut motions.

Assertion (A) — Correct: Expenditure charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India is non-votable. Items such as the salaries of the President, CAG, Supreme Court judges, and debt service charges fall into this category. Because they are not 'voted' demands for grants, cut motions cannot be moved against them.

Reason (R) — Correct: Article 113 of the Constitution distinguishes between charged and voted expenditure. Charged items are placed before the House but cannot be put to vote — they are automatically authorised. Voted items require Parliament's approval, making them susceptible to cut motions.

Causal relationship: R directly explains A. The immunity of charged expenditure from cut motions flows from Article 113's design, which removes these items from Parliament's voting power entirely.

Correct answer: (a) — Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Charged items include: President's emoluments, Speaker/Deputy Speaker's salaries, CAG's salary, Supreme Court and High Court judges' salaries, Lok Sabha Secretariat charges, and debt obligations.
• The rationale is to protect constitutional functionaries' independence from parliamentary pressure.
• Article 112 presents the Annual Financial Statement; Article 114 governs the Appropriation Bill.

solution.concept_anchor: Budget procedural sequence including cut motions stage
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) swaps the positions of General Discussion and Voting on Demands, which many students confuse because both seem like 'debate on the budget'.
elimination_logic: Budget presentation (Railway Budget merged with Union Budget since 2017) must come first — eliminate any option not starting with budget presentation.
General discussion follows presentation: it is a broad debate on budget principles with no voting — eliminate options placing voting before general discussion.
Voting on Demands for Grants (where cut motions are moved) comes after general discussion — eliminate options reversing this.
The Appropriation Bill is introduced only after demands are voted — it consolidates all voted grants. This must come last. Option (c) reflects the correct sequence.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The temporal trap is swapping the positions of General Discussion and Voting on Demands for Grants. Both involve debate on budgetary items, and students who have not memorised the precise sequence often place voting before general discussion. The Appropriation Bill's position at the end is usually correctly recalled, making the middle sequence the decisive test point.
solution.final_explanation:
The Union Budget follows a constitutionally and procedurally defined sequence in Parliament. Understanding where cut motions fit is essential.

Correct sequence: Budget Presentation → General Discussion → Voting on Demands for Grants → Appropriation Bill → Finance Bill.

• Budget Presentation: The Finance Minister presents the budget; the House does not vote at this stage.
• General Discussion: A broad debate on budgetary proposals occurs over several days; no voting takes place, no cut motions are moved.
• Voting on Demands for Grants: Each ministry's demand is taken up; this is the stage where cut motions are moved, discussed (subject to time), and voted upon.
• Appropriation Bill: Once demands are voted (with or without cuts), they are consolidated into the Appropriation Bill under Article 114. No money can be drawn from the Consolidated Fund without this Act.
• Finance Bill: Contains tax proposals; passed after the Appropriation Bill.

Value Addition:
• Cut motions can only be moved at the Voting on Demands stage — not during General Discussion or on the Appropriation Bill itself.
• The guillotine operates at the close of the Voting on Demands stage.
• The Appropriation Bill is a Money Bill; Rajya Sabha cannot amend it.

solution.concept_anchor: Guillotine effect on pending cut motions
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students may believe that cut motions, once admitted by the Speaker, survive the guillotine and are voted upon separately.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable principle: when allotted time for demands expires, the guillotine operates — all undiscussed demands are put to vote together.
Eliminate (a): The cut motions do not automatically become part of the Appropriation Bill — they must be voted upon during the demands stage.
Eliminate (c): Admitted cut motions do not receive a separate vote after the guillotine — they lapse along with undiscussed demands unless voted within the allotted time.
Eliminate (d): The Speaker does not extend the session for pending cut motions as a matter of standard procedure. Option (b) correctly states they lapse without discussion or a separate vote.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap exploits the reasonable assumption that formally admitted motions must receive a vote. Students think the Speaker's admission creates a procedural obligation to hold a vote. In reality, the guillotine extinguishes pending cut motions along with undiscussed demands — they are simply put to vote en bloc without any debate, making the substantive purpose of the cut motion entirely moot.
solution.final_explanation:
The guillotine is a parliamentary device that preserves legislative time at the cost of substantive financial scrutiny. When the time allocated for discussion of demands for grants expires, the Speaker puts all remaining demands — and any cut motions pending against them — to vote simultaneously without further debate.

In the scenario, the opposition had moved cut motions against three ministry demands. When the allotted time expired before those demands were reached, the guillotine operated. The correct outcome is:

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Cut motions do not migrate to the Appropriation Bill; they must be resolved at the demands stage.
• Option (b) — Correct: The pending cut motions lapse without discussion and the demands are voted upon en bloc. This is the standard guillotine effect.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: There is no provision for a separate post-guillotine vote on admitted cut motions.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Extending the session solely to accommodate cut motions is not standard parliamentary procedure.

Value Addition:
• The guillotine is the primary reason cut motions are considered largely ineffective in practice.
• The guillotine originated in the UK House of Commons as a time-management tool.
• Departmentally Related Standing Committees are considered a more effective financial oversight mechanism precisely because the guillotine undermines cut motion debates.

solution.concept_anchor: Cut motion vs no-confidence motion procedural distinctions
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students know cut motions relate to confidence and may wrongly believe that the explicit no-confidence motion under Rule 198 also requires the Speaker's admissibility assessment in the same manner as cut motions.
elimination_logic: Identify the category being tested: procedural features shared among cut motions, no-confidence motions, and censure motions.
Options (b), (c), (d) all relate to mechanisms of parliamentary accountability over the executive operating in Lok Sabha.

Option (a) — A no-confidence motion requires support of at least 50 members for the Speaker to admit it (Rule 198); cut motions do not have this 50-member threshold requirement. This is the feature that does NOT apply to cut motions.
Since the question asks which feature does not characterise a cut motion, option (a) — the 50-member support requirement — is the odd feature; it belongs to no-confidence motions, not cut motions.
solution.final_explanation:
Cut motions are parliamentary instruments to oppose specific demands for grants. They have their own admissibility conditions distinct from no-confidence motions.

• Option (a) — Odd one out: The requirement of support from at least 50 members before the Speaker admits the motion is a feature of a no-confidence motion under Rule 198, not of cut motions. Cut motions are admitted by the Speaker based on the admissibility conditions in Rules 209–221 — no minimum member support is required.
• Option (b) — Applies to cut motions: Cut motions must be admitted by the Speaker based on prescribed admissibility conditions.
• Option (c) — Applies to cut motions: Cut motions can only be moved in Lok Sabha, not Rajya Sabha.
• Option (d) — Applies to cut motions: Passage of a cut motion historically implied lack of parliamentary confidence in the government's financial management.

Value Addition:
• No-confidence motion (Rule 198): needs 50 members' support for Speaker's admission.
• Cut motions: Speaker admits based on rules — no threshold of member support needed.
• A censure motion must state reasons; a Policy Cut Motion does not require elaborate reasoning — just the reduction to Re. 1.

solution.concept_anchor: Censure motion vs cut motion — target and stage differences

statement_analysis.statement: A censure motion must state reasons for censuring the minister or the council, whereas a Policy Cut Motion does not require elaborate reasons — the reduction of a demand to Re. 1 itself signals disapproval.
statement_analysis.reason: A censure motion must explicitly state the grounds on which the minister is censured. A Policy Cut Motion only needs to propose a reduction to Re. 1 as the mechanism of disapproval — no elaborate reasoning is mandated in the motion text.

statement_analysis.statement: A censure motion, if passed, leads to the automatic resignation of the entire Council of Ministers, just as the passage of a no-confidence motion does.
statement_analysis.reason: A censure motion can be directed against an individual minister or a group of ministers. Its passage carries political weight but does not constitutionally mandate the resignation of the entire Council of Ministers — unlike a no-confidence motion.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 1 is correct and students who do not carefully read Statement 2's claim about 'automatic resignation of the entire Council' may accept it as equivalent to a no-confidence motion's effect.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Censure motions must specify reasons; Policy Cut Motions operate through the Re. 1 reduction mechanism without requiring elaborate reasoning. Statement 1 is CORRECT.

Evaluate Statement 2: A censure motion does not constitutionally compel the resignation of the entire Council of Ministers — that is the consequence of a no-confidence motion under Article 75. Statement 2 is INCORRECT.
Statement 1 correct + Statement 2 incorrect → select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 conflates the consequences of a censure motion with those of a no-confidence motion. A partially prepared student who knows that parliamentary motions can bring down governments will equate a censure motion's passage with automatic resignation of the Council, not realising that censure is a weaker instrument that carries moral/political pressure but not the constitutional force of a no-confidence motion.
solution.final_explanation:
Censure motions and cut motions are distinct instruments of parliamentary control that operate at different targets and stages.

• Statement 1 — Correct: A censure motion must contain explicit grounds for censure. A Policy Cut Motion, by contrast, achieves its purpose through the symbolic reduction to Re. 1, which itself communicates policy rejection — no elaborate justification is required in the motion text.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: A censure motion can target an individual minister or the council collectively, but its passage does not trigger constitutional obligation for the entire Council to resign. It carries political pressure. Only a no-confidence motion under Article 75(3) read with parliamentary convention requires the Council to resign.

Value Addition:
• A censure motion may be moved against an individual minister; a no-confidence motion targets the entire Council of Ministers.
• Passage of a cut motion historically implied loss of confidence but is not constitutionally equivalent to a no-confidence motion.
• India does not have a constitutional provision explicitly defining what happens when a censure motion passes — it is governed by convention.

• The Speaker's discretionary power to admit, modify, or disallow a cut motion flows from Rules 209–221.
• Understanding rule numbers is useful for UPSC questions on parliamentary procedure that test precise knowledge.

statement_analysis.reason: Supplementary Demands for Grants, like the main budget demands, are voted upon in Lok Sabha and are therefore susceptible to cut motions under the same procedural rules.

statement_analysis.statement: Cut motions cannot be moved on a Vote on Account because it is only an interim authorisation and does not constitute a regular demand for grants.
statement_analysis.reason: A Vote on Account, though an interim measure, is still a voting exercise on demands for grants in Lok Sabha — cut motions can technically be moved at this stage as well.

statement_analysis.statement: Excess Grants, which are presented to Parliament after the year-end audit by the CAG, also go through the standard Voting on Demands stage and are therefore unambiguously subject to cut motions.
statement_analysis.reason: The applicability of cut motions to Excess Grants is a procedurally nuanced question. Excess Grants under Article 115 are presented after the financial year ends and the actual expenditure has already occurred, making the practical scope of cut motions on them debatable and not unambiguously settled.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) '1 only' is a strong distractor because students who know the main trap (Vote on Account exemption) but incorrectly accept it as true will eliminate Statement 2 and end up at (a), not realising Statement 2 is the false claim.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Supplementary demands follow the same voting procedure as main demands — cut motions apply. Statement 1 is CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: Vote on Account is voted upon in Lok Sabha; cut motions can technically be moved against it. The claim that they 'cannot' be moved is incorrect. Statement 2 is INCORRECT.

Evaluate Statement 3: Excess Grants are a nuanced case — since expenditure has already occurred, the scope of cut motions is not unambiguously clear or universally settled. Calling it 'unambiguously subject' overstates. Statement 3 is INCORRECT.
Only Statement 1 is correct — select option (a)... wait: re-checking options: (a) 1 only, (b) 1 and 2 only, (c) 2 and 3 only, (d) 1 and 3 only. Only Statement 1 is correct — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap in Statement 2 exploits the widespread assumption that Vote on Account, being interim and limited, is somehow exempt from cut motions. In reality, Vote on Account is still voted upon by Lok Sabha and cut motions can apply. Statement 3's trap is subtler — it uses the word 'unambiguously' to turn a contested procedural question into a false certainty, trapping students who know Excess Grants exist but are unaware of the nuance around cut motions applying post-expenditure.
solution.final_explanation:
The scope of cut motions extends beyond the main annual budget to other financial instruments that go through the voting stage in Lok Sabha.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Supplementary Demands for Grants are presented when the original appropriation falls short. They pass through the Voting on Demands stage and are subject to cut motions under the same rules.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: A Vote on Account is an interim authorisation enabling the government to draw from the Consolidated Fund pending the full budget's passage. Since it involves voting in Lok Sabha, cut motions can technically be moved — the claim of categorical inapplicability is wrong.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: Excess Grants under Article 115 are presented after the financial year when spending has already occurred. Whether cut motions apply to them is procedurally uncertain and debatable — characterising it as 'unambiguous' is an overstatement.

Value Addition:
• Vote on Account: typically covers two months' expenditure at one-sixth of the annual estimate.
• Supplementary Demands under Article 115 are also a Money Bill — Rajya Sabha cannot amend them.
• Excess Grants require regularisation by Parliament but the practical scope of cut motions on post-facto expenditure is limited.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 114 Appropriation Act — sequence with cut motions
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because students correctly know Article 114 relates to Appropriation Bills but may conflate 'no money shall be withdrawn' with 'no demand shall be voted' — slightly shifting the provision's exact operative clause.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): The statement that cut motions can be moved on the Appropriation Bill itself is incorrect — cut motions must be decided before the Appropriation Bill is introduced.

Retain (b): Article 114 mandates that no money may be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund except under an Appropriation Act — this correctly describes the provision and its sequencing relationship with cut motions.
Eliminate (c): Appropriation Bill is a Money Bill under Article 110 — Rajya Sabha cannot amend it; this pairing is incorrect as stated.
Eliminate (d): The Appropriation Bill does not consolidate tax proposals — the Finance Bill does that. The Appropriation Bill consolidates voted grants.
solution.final_explanation:
The Appropriation Bill and Article 114 form the constitutional foundation for government spending after the voting stage.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Cut motions cannot be moved on the Appropriation Bill. They must be moved and decided during the Voting on Demands for Grants stage, which precedes the introduction of the Appropriation Bill.
• Option (b) — Correct: Article 114 provides that no money shall be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund of India except under an Appropriation Act passed by Parliament. This is why the Appropriation Bill must be passed after demands are voted — it gives legislative authority to the government's spending.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Appropriation Bill is certified as a Money Bill under Article 110, not under Article 112 (which presents the Annual Financial Statement).
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Tax proposals are contained in the Finance Bill, not the Appropriation Bill. The Appropriation Bill consolidates only the voted demands for grants and charged expenditure.

Value Addition:
• The Appropriation Bill cannot be amended by Rajya Sabha.
• Voted demands + charged expenditure are both incorporated in the Appropriation Bill.
• Cut motions, if passed, reduce the amount incorporated into the Appropriation Bill for that demand.

solution.concept_anchor: Tenth Schedule anti-defection and cut motions

statement_analysis.statement: A member of the ruling party who votes in favour of an opposition cut motion against the party's three-line whip may attract disqualification under the Tenth Schedule of the Constitution.
statement_analysis.reason: Voting contrary to the party whip's direction on a parliamentary proceeding, including on cut motions, can attract Tenth Schedule disqualification for defection if the party has issued a formal whip.

statement_analysis.statement: The practical impact of the anti-defection law and the whip system has been to render cut motions largely ineffective as tools of financial accountability under majority or coalition governments.
statement_analysis.reason: When the ruling party issues a three-line whip directing members to vote against opposition cut motions, the anti-defection law's threat of disqualification ensures compliance, making it virtually impossible for cut motions to pass.

statement_analysis.statement: The anti-defection law under the Tenth Schedule applies exclusively to voting on no-confidence motions and does not extend to votes on cut motions or other financial business.
statement_analysis.reason: The Tenth Schedule applies to any vote in the House where a whip has been issued — it is not limited to no-confidence motions. Voting against a party whip on any matter, including cut motions, can attract disqualification.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 2 are correct and students who broadly know the anti-defection law applies widely may hastily assume Statement 3 is also correct.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Anti-defection (Tenth Schedule) applies when a member votes against the party whip. A three-line whip on a cut motion vote means defiance attracts potential disqualification. Statement 1 is CORRECT.

Evaluate Statement 2: The combination of the whip system and anti-defection law has made cut motions practically irrelevant in majority/coalition scenarios — a well-established observation. Statement 2 is CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3: The Tenth Schedule is not confined to no-confidence votes — it applies to any whipped vote in the House. Statement 3 is INCORRECT.
Statements 1 and 2 are correct; Statement 3 is incorrect — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a classic scope-restriction trap — it takes a true general principle (Tenth Schedule applies to parliamentary votes) and falsely restricts its scope to no-confidence motions only. Students who have studied anti-defection law in the context of no-confidence votes may not have explicitly verified its applicability to cut motions, making this a high-quality trap for partially prepared candidates.
solution.final_explanation:
The Tenth Schedule and the whip system have fundamentally altered the practical effectiveness of cut motions as tools of parliamentary financial control.

• Statement 1 — Correct: The Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law) disqualifies members who vote against their party's direction in the House where a whip has been issued. Ruling party members voting for opposition cut motions against a three-line whip risk disqualification — reinforcing party discipline.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The combined effect of mandatory party discipline (whip) and the legal deterrent of anti-defection has made cut motions largely theoretical in majority governments. Opposition cut motions almost never pass when the government has a working majority.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Tenth Schedule applies broadly to any vote in Parliament or a state legislature where a whip has been issued — it is not restricted to no-confidence motions. This false restriction is the trap.

Value Addition:
• The Tenth Schedule was added by the 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985.
• The Speaker decides disqualification petitions under the Tenth Schedule (Kihoto Hollohan case, 1992).
• Cut motions have actually passed in rare coalition-era situations when discipline broke down.

solution.concept_anchor: Practical ineffectiveness of cut motions — multiple factors

statement_analysis.statement: The guillotine mechanism ensures that most demands for grants are voted upon without substantive discussion, leaving cut motions as largely symbolic instruments.
statement_analysis.reason: The guillotine puts undiscussed demands to vote at the close of allotted time, rendering most cut motions ineffective by denying them debate time.

statement_analysis.statement: Departmentally Related Standing Committees are considered a more effective instrument for financial scrutiny than cut motions because they examine demands in detail before voting.
statement_analysis.reason: DRSCs examine ministry-specific demands in detail, invite expert testimony, and produce reports — providing substantive scrutiny that the cut motion process, undermined by guillotine and whip, cannot offer.

statement_analysis.statement: The whip system in majority government scenarios makes it constitutionally impossible, not merely politically difficult, for a cut motion to be passed.
statement_analysis.reason: The whip system makes passage of cut motions politically very difficult but not constitutionally impossible. It is a political convention backed by anti-defection law, not a constitutional prohibition on cut motions passing.

statement_analysis.statement: Parliamentary reform committees have recommended strengthening financial scrutiny, partly because cut motions do not function as effective checks on executive spending in practice.
statement_analysis.reason: Various parliamentary reform committees (such as those chaired by former Speakers) have noted the declining effectiveness of cut motions and recommended reforms to budget scrutiny mechanisms.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All four' is a strong distractor because Statements 1, 2, and 4 are all correct, and Statement 3's use of 'constitutionally impossible' sounds precise and authoritative enough to fool unprepared students.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Guillotine's effect on undiscussed cut motions is well-established — CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: DRSCs' superiority for financial scrutiny is a recognised reform observation — CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3: 'Constitutionally impossible' is an overstatement — the whip creates political difficulty, not a constitutional bar. Statement 3 is INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 4: Reform committee recommendations on budget scrutiny are well-documented — CORRECT. Three of four statements are correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3's trap lies in the word 'constitutionally impossible.' Students who know the anti-defection law strongly inhibits dissent on whipped votes may conflate 'virtually impossible in practice' with 'constitutionally impossible.' The anti-defection law creates a legal deterrent but does not constitutionally prevent a cut motion from passing — if members choose to vote freely (and accept disqualification risk), it remains possible.
solution.final_explanation:
The effectiveness of cut motions as tools of financial accountability has been substantially eroded in practice by multiple institutional and political factors.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Guillotine means most demands are never debated; cut motions against undiscussed demands lapse without any floor discussion — defeating their purpose.
• Statement 2 — Correct: DRSCs examine ministry demands in detail over extended periods, producing scrutiny reports that are far more substantive than the time-constrained cut motion process.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The whip system backed by anti-defection law makes it extremely difficult politically, but there is no constitutional prohibition. Rare instances of cut motions passing (e.g., UPA-era episodes) demonstrate it is not constitutionally barred.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Multiple parliamentary reform recommendations have pointed to the weakness of cut motions and suggested strengthening standing committee scrutiny as a substitute.

Value Addition:
• DRSCs were constituted in 1993 — their creation partly acknowledged cut motions' practical ineffectiveness.
• Cut motions have passed on rare occasions, notably during coalition governments with thin majorities.
• Strengthening financial committees is a recurring recommendation in parliamentary reform discourse.

solution.concept_anchor: Passage of cut motion vs. automatic fall of government — UPSC trap
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes. A cut motion targets a specific demand for grants, while a no-confidence motion targets the entire Council of Ministers — they are distinct instruments with different scope.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? No. The passage of a cut motion does not automatically and constitutionally require the government to resign. This is a matter of historical convention, not a firm constitutional mandate — and modern practice treats cut motions as separable from confidence votes.
Step 3 — Since R is incorrect, causal relationship is moot.
A is correct + R is incorrect → select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Reason (R) is the central UPSC trap: students who have studied cut motions superficially often recall the statement that 'passage of a cut motion equals a vote of no-confidence' without recognising that this is a historical convention, not a firm constitutional rule. Modern Indian parliamentary practice has seen cut motions passed without governments resigning — the constitutional convention is not absolute. Asserting that passage 'automatically requires the government to resign' overstates the constitutional position and makes R incorrect.
solution.final_explanation:
The relationship between cut motions and the fate of the government is one of the most commonly tested and misunderstood aspects of Indian parliamentary procedure.

Assertion (A) — Correct: A cut motion operates at the level of a specific demand for grants — it is a targeted financial instrument. A no-confidence motion, by contrast, is a comprehensive indictment of the entire Council of Ministers and is moved under Rule 198. They are structurally distinct.

Reason (R) — Incorrect: The claim that passage of a cut motion 'automatically and constitutionally' requires the government to resign overstates the position. Historically, the convention was that defeat on a cut motion implied loss of confidence. However, this is a constitutional convention — not an explicit constitutional mandate. Modern Indian political practice has seen instances where governments survived cut motion defeats by treating them as accidents of coalition arithmetic rather than formal confidence votes. There is no provision in the Constitution that equates a cut motion defeat with a mandatory obligation to resign.

Correct answer: (c) — A is correct but R is incorrect.

Value Addition:
• Rule 198 governs no-confidence motions — requires support of 50 members.
• Article 75(3): Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to Lok Sabha — but operationalised through no-confidence motions, not cut motions.
• UPA government (2009): experienced cut motion defeats without treating them as confidence votes.

solution.concept_anchor: Token Cut Rs. 100 vs Economy Cut specific amount — key distinction

statement_analysis.statement: A Token Cut Motion proposes reduction of a demand by Rs. 100 to signal that the proposed expenditure is wasteful, while an Economy Cut Motion proposes reduction by a specific stated amount to ventilate a specific public grievance.
statement_analysis.reason: The purposes are exactly reversed: the Token Cut (Rs. 100) is for airing a specific grievance, and the Economy Cut (specific stated amount) signals that expenditure is excessive or wasteful.

statement_analysis.statement: In an Economy Cut Motion, the precise amount by which the demand is to be reduced must be specified within the motion itself.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a mandatory procedural requirement — the Economy Cut Motion must state the exact rupee amount of reduction; a vague or unspecified reduction amount would render it inadmissible.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because Statement 2 is correct and students who confirm that may accept Statement 1 as also possibly correct without carefully checking the reversal of purposes.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The description reverses the purposes — Token Cut is for specific grievance (Rs. 100), Economy Cut is for wasteful expenditure (specific amount). Statement 1 is INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: Economy Cut Motions must specify the amount of reduction within the motion — this is a well-established procedural requirement. Statement 2 is CORRECT.
Statement 1 incorrect + Statement 2 correct → select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 1 is a deliberate reversal of the purposes of Token Cut and Economy Cut motions — the classic conflation trap. Students who have memorised that 'Rs. 100 = Token' and 'specific amount = Economy' but have not fixed the purpose against each type will read Statement 1 quickly and miss the reversal, especially under exam pressure. The sentence is grammatically smooth and authoritative-sounding, which heightens the trap's effectiveness.
solution.final_explanation:
Token Cut and Economy Cut motions are frequently confused because both involve 'reductions' that seem financial in nature. The key is to remember that purpose and amount are distinct features of each type.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: The statement reverses the purposes of the two cut motions. A Token Cut Motion reduces the demand by Rs. 100 to raise a specific public grievance within the government's sphere of responsibility. An Economy Cut Motion proposes reduction by a specific stated amount to indicate that the projected expenditure is excessive or wasteful — not to ventilate a grievance.
• Statement 2 — Correct: A procedural requirement for the Economy Cut Motion is that the amount of proposed reduction must be explicitly stated within the motion. This makes the opposition's fiscal objection specific and quantified.

Value Addition:
• Memory aid: Token (Rs. 100) = Grievance; Economy (specific ₹) = Wasteful spending; Policy (Re. 1) = Policy rejection.
• The grievance in a Token Cut must fall within the government's direct sphere of responsibility.
• All three types are subject to the same admissibility conditions under Lok Sabha Rules 209–221.

solution.concept_anchor: Cut motions in state legislatures — Vidhan Sabha only
solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is a strong distractor because students who know both chambers exist in bicameral states may assume both houses participate in financial scrutiny, paralleling the misconception about Rajya Sabha.
elimination_logic: Eliminate (a): Both chambers cannot move cut motions — only the lower house (Vidhan Sabha) has this power, mirroring the Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha dynamic.
Eliminate (c): Vidhan Parishad (upper house) cannot move cut motions — it has no power to vote on state budget demands, analogous to Rajya Sabha's position.
Eliminate (d): The power to move cut motions is not reserved for the Opposition — any member of the Vidhan Sabha can move a cut motion subject to admissibility.
Retain (b): Only the Vidhan Sabha (lower house) of a bicameral state legislature can move cut motions on state budget demands.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap replaces 'Vidhan Sabha' with 'Vidhan Parishad' or uses both chambers, exploiting students' uncertainty about which state chamber mirrors which central chamber. The Vidhan Parishad, like the Rajya Sabha, has no power over money bills and cannot vote on state budget demands — making cut motions exclusively a Vidhan Sabha instrument.
solution.final_explanation:
State legislatures mirror the Lok Sabha–Rajya Sabha dynamic in financial matters. The Vidhan Sabha (state lower house) is the primary financial authority.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Members of both Vidhan Sabha and Vidhan Parishad cannot jointly move cut motions. Only Vidhan Sabha members can.
• Option (b) — Correct: Cut motions on state budget demands can only be moved in the Vidhan Sabha. The Vidhan Parishad, where it exists, has no power to vote on state demands for grants, mirroring Rajya Sabha's exclusion at the Union level.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Vidhan Parishad members cannot move cut motions — the Vidhan Parishad plays no role in voting on state budget demands.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: Any member of the Vidhan Sabha — not just the Opposition — may move a cut motion, subject to the Speaker's admissibility determination.

Value Addition:
• Six states currently have Vidhan Parishads (bicameral legislatures): UP, Bihar, Maharashtra, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana.
• In unicameral states (only Vidhan Sabha), the question of Vidhan Parishad exclusion does not arise.
• State-level cut motions have caused political crises and floor test situations in coalition governments.

solution.concept_anchor: Nature and purpose of cut motions as financial check

statement_analysis.statement: A cut motion is a legislative instrument that enables Parliament to oppose a specific demand for grants as part of its oversight of executive financial power.
statement_analysis.reason: This accurately describes the fundamental nature of a cut motion — it is targeted at a specific demand for grants and serves as a check on executive financial authority.

statement_analysis.statement: Opposing a demand through a cut motion has the same legal effect as rejecting the entire Union Budget, since both prevent the government from drawing funds from the Consolidated Fund.
statement_analysis.reason: A cut motion targets only the specific demand to which it relates; rejection of the entire budget would require defeating the Appropriation Bill as a whole. The two instruments have entirely different scope and legal effect.

statement_analysis.statement: The passage of a cut motion reduces the amount available to the government under the specific head of expenditure it targets, without affecting other demands for grants.
statement_analysis.reason: When a cut motion passes, it reduces only the demand to which it relates — other demands are unaffected. The reduced amount is subsequently incorporated into the Appropriation Bill.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) '1 and 3 only' is actually correct — wait: re-checking: (a) 1 and 2 only, (b) 2 and 3 only, (c) 1 and 3 only, (d) 1, 2 and 3. Statements 1 and 3 are correct and Statement 2 is incorrect → correct answer is (c) '1 and 3 only'.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Cut motions oppose specific demands for grants as a check on executive financial power — this is the textbook definition. CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: Equating a cut motion with budget rejection is false — a cut motion affects only one demand; the budget involves all appropriations. INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3: Passage of a cut motion reduces only the targeted demand without affecting others — this is precisely how the mechanism operates. CORRECT.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statement 2 incorrect — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 exploits a scope-extension error — it extends the effect of a cut motion (which applies to one demand) to the entire budget. Students who have not carefully distinguished the targeted nature of cut motions from the wholesale rejection of budget appropriations will find Statement 2 plausible, especially since both ultimately involve 'preventing government from drawing funds.'
solution.final_explanation:
Cut motions are instruments of targeted financial control, not wholesale budget rejection.

• Statement 1 — Correct: A cut motion is precisely defined as an instrument to oppose a specific demand for grants. It is one of the few direct mechanisms through which the legislature checks the executive's proposed expenditure on a demand-by-demand basis.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Opposing one demand through a cut motion is qualitatively and legally different from rejecting the entire budget. The latter would involve defeating the Appropriation Bill, which consolidates all demands. A cut motion leaves all other demands intact.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The passage of a cut motion reduces only the specific demand targeted. The reduced figure is then incorporated into the Appropriation Bill — other ministry demands remain unaffected.

Value Addition:
• Cut motions are demand-specific — each motion addresses one ministry's demand.
• India's budget system was earlier presented in two parts (Railway Budget + Union Budget); merged from 2017 onwards.
• The Appropriation Bill as passed must correspond exactly to the sum of all voted demands (as modified by any cut motions) plus charged items.

solution.concept_anchor: Policy Cut — Re. 1 reduction signals policy disapproval
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because Rs. 100 is associated with a cut motion (Token Cut) and students who have partially memorised the amounts may place it here instead of Re. 1.
elimination_logic: Recall: Policy Cut = demand reduced to Re. 1 (signalling policy disapproval).
Eliminate (a): Zero rupees would mean demand is rejected entirely — this is not how Policy Cut operates.
Eliminate (b): Rs. 100 is the Token Cut reduction amount for grievance ventilation — not policy disapproval.
Eliminate (c): A specific stated amount is the Economy Cut's feature — not the Policy Cut. Retain (d): Re. 1 is the correct amount for the Policy Cut Motion.
solution.final_explanation:
The Policy Cut Motion is the most symbolically potent of the three types of cut motions. It communicates parliamentary rejection of the policy underpinning a demand.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Reducing demand to zero would amount to eliminating the demand entirely — this is not the mechanism of a Policy Cut.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Rs. 100 is associated with the Token Cut Motion, which ventilates a specific grievance — not policy disapproval.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Reduction by a specific stated amount is the feature of the Economy Cut Motion, signalling wasteful expenditure.
• Option (d) — Correct: The Policy Cut Motion proposes that the demand be reduced to Re. 1. This symbolic figure communicates that Parliament disapproves of the entire policy behind the demand — the government should reconsider the policy before seeking funds.

Value Addition:
• The Re. 1 amount is purely symbolic — it does not actually fund any activity but communicates the legislature's policy objection.
• Even if a Policy Cut Motion passes, the government must revisit the policy; it does not mean the programme is permanently cancelled.
• Opposition parties strategically use Policy Cut Motions to force floor debates on contentious policy failures.

solution.concept_anchor: Government response options when cut motion passes

statement_analysis.statement: Cut motions have never been passed in the Indian Parliament since Independence, as the whip system has always ensured government majorities.
statement_analysis.reason: Cut motions have passed on rare occasions, notably during coalition governments with thin or unreliable majorities, such as during the UPA era when ruling coalition members voted with the opposition.

statement_analysis.statement: When a cut motion passes, the Indian Constitution explicitly requires the government to resign, treating the defeat as equivalent to a no-confidence vote.
statement_analysis.reason: The Constitution contains no such explicit requirement. Passage of a cut motion historically signalled loss of confidence by convention, but modern practice allows governments to treat it as separable from a formal confidence vote — there is no constitutional mandate to resign.

statement_analysis.statement: The passage of a cut motion is a strong political signal of minority status or coalition fragility, even if the government chooses to treat it as distinct from a formal no-confidence motion.
statement_analysis.reason: Politically, cut motion defeats signal that the government cannot command a reliable majority on financial business — a warning sign of coalition instability — even if the government does not constitutionally have to resign.

solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) '1 only' is a strong distractor because Statement 1 contains a bold false claim ('never been passed'), which students may hesitate to call incorrect if they are unsure about specific historical instances.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Cut motions have passed in rare instances — notably during coalition governments. The claim 'never been passed' is INCORRECT — qualifies as NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 2: No constitutional provision mandates resignation on a cut motion defeat. The claim of 'explicit constitutional requirement' is INCORRECT — qualifies as NOT correct.
Evaluate Statement 3: The political signal argument is factually sound — cut motion defeats do indicate coalition fragility. Statement 3 is CORRECT — does not qualify as NOT correct.
Statements 1 and 2 are NOT correct — select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a high-quality trap for students who have read the phrase 'passage of a cut motion = vote of no-confidence' from textbooks and assumed this is a constitutional provision. It is a historical convention — the Constitution nowhere equates a cut motion defeat with a mandatory resignation obligation. The distinction between constitutional convention and constitutional mandate is a recurring UPSC examination point.
solution.final_explanation:
The historical record and constitutional framework governing cut motion defeats are frequently misrepresented in popular understanding.

• Statement 1 — Incorrect: Cut motions have passed in the Indian Parliament. During coalition governments, instances arose where ruling party allies voted with the opposition, leading to cut motion defeats. The UPA government faced such situations. 'Never passed' is factually wrong.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: There is no explicit constitutional provision requiring the government to resign upon a cut motion defeat. Article 75(3) establishes collective responsibility to Lok Sabha, but this is operationalised through a formal no-confidence motion, not automatically through a cut motion defeat. Governments have survived cut motion defeats by treating them as management lapses rather than confidence votes.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Politically, a cut motion defeat reveals that the government cannot reliably muster its numbers — a signal of coalition fragility or a minority situation, warranting political attention even without constitutional compulsion to resign.

Value Addition:
• India has no explicit constitutional provision equating cut motion defeat with mandatory resignation.
• Article 75(3) collective responsibility is enforced through no-confidence motions under Rule 198.
• Coalition-era India (1989–2014) was more susceptible to cut motion defeats than single-party majority periods.

solution.concept_anchor: Admissibility — cut motion must not make assumptions about government policy
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because the sub-judice condition is well-known and students may apply it broadly without checking whether the scenario specifically mentions a pending judicial proceeding.
elimination_logic: Identify the applicable rule: A cut motion is inadmissible if it makes assumptions about or comments on government policy beyond the demand itself, or if it contains arguments and inferences.
Eliminate (a): The sub-judice ground requires that the matter be pending before a court or tribunal — the scenario describes a policy disagreement, not a pending legal proceeding.
Eliminate (b): A cut motion relating to multiple demands is inadmissible — but the scenario describes a motion against a single ministry's demand. This ground does not apply.
Eliminate (d): The charged expenditure bar applies to non-votable items — the scenario involves a ministry's voted demand, not charged expenditure.

Retain (c): The admissibility condition that a cut motion must not assume a particular policy course or contain arguments and inferences is violated when the motion's text assumes that the government 'must immediately reverse' its policy — this constitutes an argument or inference embedded in the motion.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (a) is the planned distractor — students who recall 'sub-judice = inadmissible' may apply it reflexively without checking whether the scenario mentions a pending court case. The actual bar triggered in this scenario is the prohibition on arguments and inferences in the motion text — a less commonly recalled admissibility condition that catches well-prepared but not precisely prepared students.
solution.final_explanation:
The admissibility of cut motions is governed by multiple conditions. A key condition is that the motion must be clearly expressed and must not contain arguments, inferences, or assumptions about government policy.

In the scenario, the cut motion's text assumes that the government 'must immediately reverse its industrial policy' — this embeds an argument or inference into the motion itself, which is expressly prohibited under Lok Sabha Rules 209–221. The Speaker would disallow it on this ground.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The sub-judice bar requires a pending court or tribunal proceeding. The scenario involves a policy dispute — no judicial proceeding is mentioned.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: The single-demand rule is not violated — the motion targets one ministry's specific demand.
• Option (c) — Correct: A cut motion must not make assumptions about government policy or contain arguments and inferences. A motion asserting that the government 'must immediately reverse' its policy does exactly that — it embeds an argument, making it inadmissible.
• Option (d) — Incorrect: The charged expenditure bar applies to non-votable items (President's salary, judges' salaries, etc.) — a Ministry of Commerce demand is a voted item.

Value Addition:
• Other admissibility bars: relates to more than one demand; defamatory statements; irrelevant matter; supersedes notices already received by the House.
• Speaker's admission is discretionary — admissibility conditions set the threshold but the Speaker may also disallow on other grounds.
• Motion text must be confined to expressing disapproval, not dictating the policy alternative.

solution.concept_anchor: Correct identification of cut motion type from description

statement_analysis.statement: A motion proposing that the demand for grants of the Ministry of Jal Shakti be reduced to Re. 1 on the ground that the government's water conservation policy has failed.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a Policy Cut Motion — reduction to Re. 1 signals disapproval of the policy underlying the demand. The description matches precisely.

statement_analysis.statement: A motion proposing that the demand for grants of the Ministry of Agriculture be reduced by Rs. 500 crore on the ground that the proposed allocation for fertiliser subsidies is excessive.
statement_analysis.reason: This is an Economy Cut Motion — a specific stated amount (Rs. 500 crore) is proposed for reduction on grounds of excessive/wasteful expenditure.

statement_analysis.statement: A motion proposing that the demand for grants of the Ministry of Health be reduced by Rs. 100 crore to draw attention to the government's failure to operationalise new AIIMS hospitals.
statement_analysis.reason: This describes what sounds like a Token Cut (specific grievance) but proposes Rs. 100 crore — not Rs. 100. Rs. 100 crore is a specific stated amount characteristic of an Economy Cut, not a Token Cut. The description combines Economy Cut amount with Token Cut purpose, making this an improperly characterised motion.

statement_analysis.statement: A motion proposing that the demand for grants of the Ministry of Railways be reduced by Rs. 100 to raise the matter of inadequate safety inspections on the Konkan Railway route.
statement_analysis.reason: This is a Token Cut Motion — Rs. 100 reduction, specific public grievance (safety inspections), within the government's sphere of responsibility. All three elements of a Token Cut are satisfied.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) 'All four' is a strong distractor because Statements 1, 2, and 4 are correctly described and students may hastily accept Statement 3 without noticing that Rs. 100 crore is not the same as Rs. 100.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: Re. 1 reduction + policy failure = Policy Cut Motion correctly described. CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: Rs. 500 crore + excessive expenditure = Economy Cut Motion correctly described. CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3: Rs. 100 crore is NOT the Token Cut amount — Token Cut requires Rs. 100, not Rs. 100 crore. This conflates Token purpose with Economy amount. INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 4: Rs. 100 reduction + specific grievance (safety inspections) = Token Cut Motion correctly described. CORRECT. Three statements correct — select option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is a precision trap: students see 'Rs. 100' at first glance and think 'Token Cut' without reading the full figure 'Rs. 100 crore.' The Token Cut requires exactly Rs. 100 — not Rs. 100 crore. This exploits rapid reading under exam pressure and conflates the symbolic Rs. 100 figure with a large budget number that merely happens to contain '100' in its description.
solution.final_explanation:
Identifying the correct type of cut motion from a description requires attention to both the amount proposed and the stated purpose.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Policy Cut Motion. Re. 1 + policy disapproval = textbook definition met.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Economy Cut Motion. Rs. 500 crore (specific stated amount) + excessive expenditure claim = Economy Cut definition met.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The amount proposed is Rs. 100 crore, not Rs. 100. The Token Cut Motion requires a symbolic reduction of exactly Rs. 100 — a four-digit figure, not a crore-level figure. Rs. 100 crore with a grievance-ventilation purpose does not fit any type cleanly; it resembles an Economy Cut by amount but a Token Cut by purpose — an internally inconsistent description.
• Statement 4 — Correct: Token Cut Motion. Rs. 100 reduction + specific grievance (safety inspections on Konkan Railway) within government's responsibility = Token Cut definition met precisely.

Value Addition:
• Token Cut's Rs. 100 is purely symbolic — it represents parliamentary attention, not fiscal intent.
• Economy Cut's amount must be specific — vague language like 'substantial amount' would fail admissibility.
• All three types can be moved simultaneously against different aspects of the same ministry's demand.

solution.concept_anchor: Guillotine mechanism and undiscussed cut motions

statement_analysis.statement: The guillotine in Indian parliamentary practice refers to the mechanism by which undiscussed demands for grants are put to vote together at the close of the time allotted for the Voting on Demands stage.
statement_analysis.reason: This is the standard definition of the guillotine as applied in Indian Parliament — undiscussed demands are voted en bloc when allotted time expires.

statement_analysis.statement: When the guillotine operates, cut motions that had been admitted by the Speaker but not reached for discussion are voted upon individually before the undiscussed demands.
statement_analysis.reason: Admitted cut motions that are not reached for discussion lapse along with the undiscussed demands when the guillotine operates — they are not voted upon individually; the demand itself is voted en bloc.

statement_analysis.statement: The guillotine is one of the primary institutional reasons why cut motions are considered practically ineffective as scrutiny tools, despite being theoretically powerful instruments of financial control.
statement_analysis.reason: The guillotine denies cut motions their debate platform, rendering them ineffective in practice — this is a widely accepted critique of the Indian budget process.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) '1, 2 and 3' is a strong distractor because Statements 1 and 3 are correct and Statement 2 sounds procedurally plausible — students may assume admitted motions receive at least a separate vote.
elimination_logic: Evaluate Statement 1: The guillotine = undiscussed demands voted en bloc at close of allotted time. Standard and correct definition. CORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 2: Admitted but undiscussed cut motions do NOT receive individual votes — they lapse with the undiscussed demands when guillotine operates. INCORRECT.
Evaluate Statement 3: Guillotine as a reason for cut motion ineffectiveness is well-established. CORRECT.
Statements 1 and 3 correct; Statement 2 incorrect — select option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 targets students who assume that once a motion is formally admitted by the Speaker, procedural fairness demands it receive at least a vote. The admission by the Speaker is only a threshold determination on admissibility — it does not create a procedural obligation for separate voting. The guillotine's operation is mechanical and time-based; it overrides all pending motions.
solution.final_explanation:
The guillotine is a time-management device that effectively neutralises most cut motions before they can be debated or voted upon meaningfully.

• Statement 1 — Correct: When the allotted time for the Voting on Demands stage expires, the Speaker puts all undiscussed demands to vote simultaneously — this is the guillotine. No debate precedes these votes.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: Admitted cut motions that were not reached during discussion do not receive separate votes. They lapse along with the undiscussed demands. The guillotine is an omnibus mechanism — it does not create carve-outs for admitted motions.
• Statement 3 — Correct: The guillotine is consistently cited as the primary practical reason why cut motions fail as scrutiny tools. Their theoretical power is undermined by the reality that most demands are guillotined.

Value Addition:
• The guillotine device originated in the UK Parliament — introduced to manage filibustering.
• In the Indian budget calendar, only a handful of ministries' demands are actually discussed before being voted; the rest are guillotined.
• DRSCs were created partly as a compensatory mechanism for the scrutiny deficit caused by the guillotine.

solution.concept_anchor: Comparative features — cut motion vs censure vs no-confidence
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is a strong distractor because it correctly places items A and B but swaps the admission thresholds for cut motion and no-confidence motion — the exact distinction students are least likely to have memorised precisely.
elimination_logic: Anchor: No-confidence motion (C) — requires 50 members' support for Speaker's admission under Rule 198. C-3 is confirmed.
Cut motion (A) — admitted by the Speaker based on admissibility conditions in Rules 209–221; no member threshold. A-2 is confirmed.
Censure motion (B) — must state explicit reasons for censuring; can target an individual minister. B-1 is confirmed.
Policy Cut Motion (D) — reduces demand to Re. 1 as the mechanism of expressing policy disapproval. D-4 is confirmed. Select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap is in pairing the admission conditions: students who broadly know both cut motions and no-confidence motions require Speaker involvement may swap the '50 members support' requirement — correctly belonging to no-confidence — with cut motion admissibility. Precise recall of which instrument needs the 50-member threshold is the differentiator here.
solution.final_explanation:
Distinguishing cut motions from censure and no-confidence motions on procedural grounds is a high-frequency UPSC test area.

• A (Cut Motion) — 2: Admitted by the Speaker based on prescribed admissibility conditions (Rules 209–221). No minimum member support threshold is required for admission.
• B (Censure Motion) — 1: Must explicitly state reasons for censuring the minister or council. Can be directed against an individual minister, unlike a no-confidence motion.
• C (No-Confidence Motion) — 3: Requires support of at least 50 members before the Speaker can admit it for consideration under Rule 198 of Lok Sabha.
• D (Policy Cut Motion) — 4: Proposes reduction of the demand to Re. 1, symbolically communicating Parliament's rejection of the policy underlying that demand.

Value Addition:
• A censure motion's passage does not constitutionally compel the entire Council to resign — unlike a no-confidence motion.
• Cut motions cannot be moved against charged expenditure items.
• No-confidence motion under Article 75(3) is the constitutional mechanism for collective responsibility — Rule 198 operationalises it.

solution.concept_anchor: Vote on Account susceptibility to cut motions
elimination_logic: Step 1 — Is Assertion (A) correct? Yes. A Vote on Account is voted upon by Lok Sabha — since it involves voting on demands, cut motions can technically be moved against it.

Step 2 — Is Reason (R) correct? Yes. A Vote on Account is an interim authorisation — typically covering two months' expenditure — to enable the government to meet expenses pending full budget passage.

Step 3 — Does R causally explain A? No. The fact that Vote on Account is 'interim' does not explain why cut motions can be moved. The reason cut motions can be moved is that a Vote on Account involves Lok Sabha voting on demands for grants — the interim nature is descriptive of what it is, not why cut motions apply. R describes Vote on Account accurately but does not causally explain A's claim.
Both A and R are correct, but R does NOT explain A → select option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The trap is option (a): students who verify both A and R as factually correct may hastily conclude that R explains A, since both discuss Vote on Account. In reality, R describes the nature of Vote on Account (interim, two months) while A's basis is the procedural fact that it involves Lok Sabha voting — these are logically independent claims. The 'interim' character in R is not the causal reason for cut motion applicability.
solution.final_explanation:
Vote on Account and its relationship with cut motions test understanding of both the instrument itself and the procedural basis for cut motion applicability.

Assertion (A) — Correct: A Vote on Account goes through the Voting on Demands stage in Lok Sabha. Since cut motions are instruments moved during this stage, they can technically be moved against Vote on Account demands — the scope of cut motions is not limited to the main annual budget.

Reason (R) — Correct: A Vote on Account is an interim legislative authorisation enabling the government to draw funds from the Consolidated Fund pending full budget passage. It typically covers two months' expenditure at approximately one-sixth of the annual estimate. This is an accurate description of the Vote on Account.

Causal relationship: R does NOT explain A. A is true because Vote on Account involves Lok Sabha voting on demands — making it procedurally susceptible to cut motions. R tells us the Vote on Account is 'interim' — this characterisation does not provide the causal link explaining why cut motions apply. The causal reason is the voting stage, not the interim nature.

Correct answer: (b) — Both A and R are correct, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

Value Addition:
• Vote on Account must be approved before 1 April each year to avoid a fiscal gap.
• Supplementary Demands and Additional Demands also go through voting — cut motions apply to them too.
• During election years, Vote on Account may cover a longer period (up to 4–6 months).

solution.concept_anchor: Items immune from cut motions — charged vs voted
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is a strong distractor because the salary of the CAG is charged expenditure and is immune from cut motions — but students may confuse whether High Court judges' salaries are charged or voted.
elimination_logic: Identify the category: items charged upon the Consolidated Fund that are immune from cut motions.
Salary of the President — charged expenditure, immune. Belongs to the category.
Salary of the CAG — charged expenditure, immune. Belongs to the category.
Salaries of High Court judges — charged upon the Consolidated Fund under Article 229(1). Belongs to the category.

Salary of the Attorney General of India — NOT charged upon the Consolidated Fund; the AG is a constitutional functionary but the salary is not among the explicitly charged items under Article 112. This is the odd one out — select option (d).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The Attorney General of India is a high-profile constitutional functionary (Article 76), which makes students assume the salary is charged like those of other constitutional dignitaries. However, the AG's salary is determined by the President and is not among the explicitly charged items on the Consolidated Fund under Article 112's second schedule. This entity-swap trap exploits the association between 'constitutional functionary' and 'charged expenditure.'
solution.final_explanation:
Charged expenditure encompasses specific constitutional offices whose financial independence must be protected from parliamentary pressure. Identifying which items are charged and which are not is a precision test.

• Option (a) — Belongs to the category: The salary and allowances of the President are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of India — they cannot be subject to a cut motion.
• Option (b) — Belongs to the category: The salary of the Comptroller and Auditor General is charged expenditure, reflecting the CAG's independent constitutional audit function.
• Option (c) — Belongs to the category: Salaries of High Court judges are charged upon the Consolidated Fund of the respective state (Article 229) — at the Union level, Supreme Court judges' salaries are charged under Article 112.
• Option (d) — Odd one out: The Attorney General of India, while a constitutional functionary under Article 76, does not have a salary charged upon the Consolidated Fund in the same manner as judges or the CAG. The AG's remuneration is not among the standard charged items.

Value Addition:
• Charged items: President, VP, Speaker, Deputy Speaker, CAG, SC/HC judges, Lok Sabha Secretariat, debt charges.
• Charged items are presented to Parliament but not voted — they are automatically authorised.
• Article 113 is the constitutional provision governing this distinction.
